q285.question: What is contained in the "bestowal limitations" and the further advice that Immanuel gave to Michael?
q285.answer:
Just before beginning his seventh and final bestowal on Urantia, Michael went before Immanuel, his elder brother and Paradise counselor, and handed over to him the authority of universe administration [120:0.6]. In bidding him farewell, Immanuel gave him nine directives known as the "bestowal limitations" and eight recommendations of further counsel and advice [120:1.7, 120:3.1]. These are a key to understanding many of the seemingly strange things Jesus did on earth: why he left no writings, did not marry, and did not involve himself in politics.

Underlying these directives is a single principle. In his six previous bestowals Michael had subjected himself to every phase of the will of the Supreme except the personal will of the Father, but in his seventh bestowal he had "⟦Q 120:1.2⟧elected to be wholly subject to your Father's will⟦/Q⟧" [120:1.2]. He chose to be born not as a fully developed being but as a helpless babe, divesting himself of all extraplanetary support and depending on his Paradise Father alone [120:1.1, 120:1.3].

1. The Great Purpose of the Bestowal

Immanuel told Michael that he needed to be concerned only with his unbroken communion with the Father, and that through the perfection of that relationship the whole universe would behold a new and more understandable revelation of the Father [120:1.4]. His great mission was to live a life wholeheartedly motivated to do the Father's will, thereby revealing God to the creatures of flesh and, at the same time, making a new revelation of man to God [120:2.8]. As incidental tasks he was advised to terminate the Lucifer rebellion technically as the Son of Man, to receive the title of "⟦Q 120:2.2⟧Planetary Prince of Urantia⟦/Q⟧," and to pour out the Spirit of Truth [120:2.2, 120:2.3, 120:2.6].

2. The Order of His Ministry as a Teacher

He was advised to act chiefly as a teacher to the generation of his day. First he was to liberate man's spiritual nature; next, to illuminate the darkened intellect, heal the soul, and free the mind from age-old fears; and only then to minister to physical well-being and material comfort [120:2.5]. Moreover, his life was to be lived not as a detailed example for the Urantians of his day but as an inspiration to all life on all the worlds of Nebadon [120:2.7].

3. Limits on the Use of Power

Because Michael would actually become an ordinary man while potentially remaining a Creator Son, he was warned that after the arrival of the Adjuster he should refrain from forming any will for superhuman achievement, attainment, or power [120:2.9]. At the same time he was assured that, unless he made an undivided decision as a choice of his whole personality, no superhuman repercussion would follow apart from the Father's will [120:2.9]. Meanwhile Immanuel would be responsible for the security of the universe, and he also conveyed the mandate of the Ancients of Days that any being who rebelled would be instantly annihilated [120:1.5, 120:1.6].

4. Concrete Advice about His Life

The further counsel set the direction of his everyday life. He was to follow the customs of his time in family life [120:3.3]; with regard to the social order, he was to confine his efforts to spiritual regeneration and intellectual emancipation and not become entangled in economic structures or political commitments [120:3.4]; he was not to interfere with the normal evolution of the races [120:3.5]; and he was to avoid the formation of an organized cult or a crystallized religion, so that his life and teachings might become "⟦Q 120:3.6⟧the common heritage of all religions and all peoples⟦/Q⟧" [120:3.6]. Along with the advice to "⟦Q 120:3.7⟧Não deixes documentos escritos para trás de ti, naquele planeta.⟦/Q⟧" [120:3.7] came the instruction to allow no images or likenesses of himself to be made, and he was told that he would probably not enter the marriage relation because a mandate of Sonarington forbids a bestowal Son of Paradise origin to leave human offspring behind [120:3.8]. All remaining details were left to the guidance of the indwelling Adjuster and the reason-judgment of the human mind [120:3.9].

5. What It Means for Us

These directives show that Jesus' life was a path not of miracles and power but of trust and submission. Because the Creator himself laid aside his power and lived by faith-trust, he came to know by experience the meaning of the faith he asks of his creatures [120:1.3]. The fact that Jesus left no writings and founded no particular sect reminds us that his teachings must remain open today to all religions and all peoples.

Summary

Immanuel's directives can be summed up as complete submission to the Father's will, a teacher's life that reveals the Father, restraint in the use of superhuman power, and the self-discipline of leaving behind no writings, likenesses, sects, political involvements, or offspring [120:1.2, 120:2.5, 120:2.9, 120:3.6-3.8]. Even in the hills after his baptism Jesus recalled this instruction to create no permanent record on the planet, and from then on he never wrote on anything except the sand [136:4.2].

q286.question: Jesus is said to be both God and man; how were his divinity and humanity one, and what gradually grew?
q286.answer:
The Urantia Book sets forth a very clear principle concerning the divinity and humanity of Jesus. Christ Michael, "⟦Q 120:4.2⟧while truly a dual-origin being, was not a double personality⟦/Q⟧" [120:4.2]. He was not God in association with man but God incarnate in man, and from the beginning he was one combined being [120:4.2].

The only progressive factor in this relationship was the gradual, self-conscious realization and recognition by the human mind of the fact that he was God and man [120:4.2]. In other words, what changed was not his being but his human awareness of that being.

1. He Did Not Progressively Become God

Jesus did not become God at some point in his life, nor did God become man at some decisive moment. "⟦Q 120:4.3⟧Jesus foi Deus e homem — sempre e para sempre.⟦/Q⟧" [120:4.3]. This oneness of God and man is compared to the way the Paradise Trinity of three beings is in reality one Deity [120:4.3]. Therefore nothing descended at his baptism to make him divine, nor was divinity added to him little by little as he grew.

2. The Growth of Awareness: From Infancy to Full Self-Consciousness

Immanuel told Michael that after surrendering his consciousness of personality he would "gradually" return to the recognition of his divine identity incarnate in human form [120:3.10]. He was born a helpless babe [120:1.1], and when the Thought Adjuster came at about five years of age, he, like all other children, did not know it [123:2.1]. At thirteen he spoke in the temple of his "Father's business" [125:6.7]; as a youth he struggled deeply with his relation to the Messianic prophecies [126:3.10]; and on Mount Hermon he became fully convinced that his divine nature was superior to his human nature [134:8.5]. By the time of the wedding at Cana, "⟦Q 137:4.2⟧Jesus estava agora cuidadosamente consciente a respeito da sua existência humana, da sua preexistência divina, e do status das suas naturezas, a humana e a divina, combinadas, ou fusionadas.⟦/Q⟧" [137:4.2].

3. The Process by Which Two Minds Became One

The growth on the human side was real. From the moment the Adjuster arrived until the day the relationship between the material human mind and the mind-endowment of the spirit was completed, his spiritual development was consistently progressive, and this experience was completed on the day of his baptism in the Jordan [129:4.2]. At his baptism he had reached the acme of human evolutionary ascent in mind conquest and identification with the spirit [136:2.2]. The forty days that followed were the first opportunity for the actual functioning of the two minds, now made one, and as a result the divine mind came to fully guide the human intellect spiritually [136:4.4]. After that the human mind still asked questions, but it unfailingly accepted the divine answers as the final verdict [136:9.5].

4. How the Divine Is Revealed: The Natural Way

Even in the mystery of this union, God the Father chose to manifest himself "⟦Q 120:4.6⟧in the normal, natural, and dependable way of divine acting⟦/Q⟧" [120:4.6]. That is why the citizens of the local universe regard the incarnation bestowal, in which a divine Son appears in the world through an apparently natural process, as the most interesting of miracles [120:4.5]. And we are urged never to forget that the supreme spiritual purpose of Michael's bestowal was to enhance the revelation of God [120:4.4].

5. What It Means for Us

That Jesus' human growth was real means that he knows the process of our growth from the inside. He lived the human life from infancy through adulthood to death, and he experienced even the high stage of human and Adjuster reconciliation [129:4.5]. Therefore the slow growth that takes place within us together with the Adjuster is by no means insignificant.

Summary

Jesus was not a double personality but one personality of dual origin, God and man from the very beginning [120:4.2, 120:4.3]. What grew was his human mind's awareness of this fact and its attunement with the Adjuster, a process completed through Mount Hermon, the baptism, and the forty days [134:8.5, 129:4.2, 136:4.4].

q287.question: According to The Urantia Book, who wrote the four Gospels of the New Testament, when, and under what circumstances?
q287.answer:
The final section of Paper 121 of The Urantia Book explains in concrete terms how the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John came into being. The midwayers who narrated the life of Jesus made use of the lost record of the apostle Andrew and the co-operation of celestial beings, yet they set themselves the aim of utilizing and to some extent co-ordinating these four Gospels [121:8.1].

According to that account, all four Gospels are honest pictures painted as their writers saw, remembered, or had learned, but each had different sources and readers, and each was affected by the writers' subsequent espousal of Paul's theology of Christianity [121:8.11].

1. The Gospel of Mark: The First Gospel, from Peter's Memory

John Mark left the earliest (excepting the notes of Andrew), briefest, and simplest record, and his record "⟦Q 121:8.3⟧is in reality the Gospel according to Simon Peter⟦/Q⟧" [121:8.3]. Knowing that the Master had refused to write out his teachings, Mark hesitated, but at Peter's instigation and on the petition of the church at Rome he began writing soon after Peter's death in A.D. 67 and completed it near the end of A.D. 68 [121:8.3]. Since then many passages have been taken out of this record, and later matter was added to replace the lost final one fifth. Together with the notes of Andrew and Matthew, it became the written basis of all subsequent Gospel narratives [121:8.3].

2. The Gospel of Matthew: A Record for Jewish Christians

The Gospel of Matthew was written for the edification of Jewish Christians; it constantly seeks to show that Jesus' deeds fulfilled the sayings of the prophets, and it portrays Jesus as the son of David [121:8.4]. This Gospel was written not by the apostle Matthew but by his disciple Isador. Isador wrote in Greek on the basis of Matthew's memory and of the Aramaic notes Matthew had made just after the crucifixion; attaching a teacher's name was the custom of that time, and there was no intent to deceive [121:8.5]. After the armies of Titus besieged Jerusalem in A.D. 70, he fled to Pella and wrote this Gospel in A.D. 71, having in his possession the first four fifths of Mark's Gospel [121:8.7]. The last copy of Matthew's original notes was destroyed in A.D. 416 when a Syrian monastery burned [121:8.6].

3. The Gospel of Luke: The Record of a Gentile Physician Taught by Paul

Luke, the physician of Antioch in Pisidia, was a gentile convert of Paul, and he presents the Master as "⟦Q 121:8.8⟧the friend of publicans and sinners⟦/Q⟧" [121:8.8]. He followed and learned from Paul from A.D. 47, wrote his Gospel in Achaia in A.D. 82 after Paul's death, and planned three books but died in A.D. 90, just before finishing the Acts of the Apostles [121:8.8]. Because his chief source was the story Paul had told him, Luke's Gospel is in a sense the Gospel according to Paul. In addition he interviewed scores of eyewitnesses and used a copy of Mark's Gospel, Isador's narrative, a record made by Cedes at Antioch, and a mutilated copy of notes said to be Andrew's [121:8.9].

4. The Gospel of John: A Record Inspired by John and Written by Nathan

The Gospel of John contains much of the ministry in and around Judea and Jerusalem that is not found in the other records. John the son of Zebedee did not write it himself but inspired it; in A.D. 101, with John's encouragement, Nathan, a Greek Jew from Caesarea, began the writing [121:8.10]. John supplied material from memory and by reference to the three records already in existence, and the Epistle of John was written by John himself as a covering letter for this work [121:8.10].

5. How the Urantia Book Narrative Relates to These Records

The midwayer who retold the life of Jesus states that he obtained his information from purely human sources as far as possible and resorted to superhuman records only when these were lacking [121:8.12]. His collected memoranda contain gems of thought from more than two thousand human beings who lived from the days of Jesus to the time of writing, and he says he worked more as a collector and editor than as an original narrator [121:8.13, 121:8.14].

Summary

The four Gospels took shape in this order: Mark (Peter's memory, A.D. 68), Matthew (Isador, A.D. 71), Luke (Paul's tradition, A.D. 82), and John (Nathan, after A.D. 101) [121:8.3-8.10]. The Urantia Book judges that these records, "⟦Q 121:8.11⟧imperfect as they are, have been sufficient to change the course of the history of Urantia for almost two thousand years⟦/Q⟧" [121:8.11].

q288.question: How does The Urantia Book explain the birth of Jesus, the star of Bethlehem, the wise men, and Herod's slaughter of the infants?
q288.answer:
The Urantia Book describes the birth of Jesus as a far simpler and more natural event than the traditional Christmas story. Jesus was born at noon on August 21, 7 B.C., near the caravan stable hewn out of the rock beneath the inn at Bethlehem, and was laid in a manger [122:7.7, 122:8.1]. "⟦Q 122:8.2⟧In just the same manner as all babies before that day and since have come into the world, the promised child was born⟦/Q⟧" [122:8.2], and on the eighth day he was circumcised and named Joshua (Jesus).

Gabriel's appearance to Mary is said to have been the only supernatural event in all her experience of conceiving and bearing the child of promise [122:3.4].

1. Why Bethlehem: The Census

The census of Caesar Augustus was carried out in Palestine, ruled by Herod, a year late, in 7 B.C. [122:7.1]. Joseph was not of the line of King David, but because six generations earlier his paternal ancestor had been adopted by Zadok, a direct descendant of David, he was reckoned as belonging to the "house of David" and so went to Bethlehem [122:4.3]. Mary did not have to go, but she insisted on accompanying him because she feared the child might be born while Joseph was away and she also wished to visit Elizabeth [122:7.2]. Because the inn was full, they stayed in the grain storage room in front of the mangers, and on the day after the birth they moved into the inn by exchanging quarters with a kindly person [122:7.7, 122:8.3].

2. The Angels' Song and the Worshipers

At the birth of Jesus the seraphim of Urantia sang anthems of glory over the Bethlehem manger, but those songs of praise were not heard by human ears [122:8.5]. And no shepherds or any other mortal creatures came to pay homage to the babe until the day of the arrival of the priests from Ur, who were sent by Zacharias [122:8.5].

3. The Wise Men and the Star of Bethlehem

The "wise men" were three priests from Ur in Mesopotamia. Having been told that "⟦Q 122:8.6⟧the light of life⟦/Q⟧" would appear as a babe among the Jews, they searched in vain in Jerusalem for many weeks; then they met Zacharias, went on to Bethlehem, found the babe, who was almost three weeks old, and left their gifts with Mary [122:8.6]. "⟦Q 122:8.7⟧Esses sábios homens não tiveram nenhuma estrela a guiá-los para Belém.⟦/Q⟧" [122:8.7]. On May 29, 7 B.C., there was an extraordinary conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn in the constellation of Pisces, and similar conjunctions occurred on September 29 and December 5; upon the basis of these wholly natural events the well-meaning zealots of a later generation constructed the legend of the star and the Magi [122:8.7]. The Urantia Book adds that in the era of oral transmission it was very easy for myths to become traditions and for traditions to become accepted as facts [122:8.7].

4. Herod's Slaughter of the Infants and the Flight to Egypt

Herod summoned the priests from Ur and questioned them about the new "⟦Q 122:10.1⟧king of the Jews⟦/Q⟧," and after hearing also of Simeon's song sung in the temple he tracked the family [122:10.1]. When after more than a year he still had not found them, he ordered all boy babies under two years of age in Bethlehem to be killed, and sixteen boy babies lost their lives in a single day [122:10.3]. This slaughter took place about the middle of October, 6 B.C., when Jesus was a little over a year old; a believer at Herod's court informed Zacharias, so the family left for Alexandria the night before the massacre and remained there two full years, until Herod's death [122:10.4].

5. The Application of Prophecies and the Problem of the Genealogies

The Urantia Book says that most of the so-called Messianic prophecies of the Old Testament were applied to Jesus long after his life had ended, that even the passage about a "young woman" bearing a son was changed to "virgin," and that the genealogies constructed later are, as a whole, not trustworthy as fact [122:4.4]. Moreover, nowhere in Gabriel's visit or in the dream visitation was there any mention of the house of David or of a Jewish deliverer; Jesus' mission was for all races and peoples [122:4.2].

Summary

Jesus was born an ordinary babe in Bethlehem because of the census, and those who came to see him were guided not by a star but by Zacharias: they were three priests from Ur [122:8.2, 122:8.6, 122:8.7]. Herod's massacre did take place, but the family had fled to Alexandria beforehand [122:10.3, 122:10.4]. The Urantia Book strips away the beautiful legends and shows that God came into the world in a natural way.

q289.question: What kind of education did the young Jesus receive at home, in the synagogue school, in nature, and among people?
q289.answer:
The Urantia Book relates that Jesus received a broad education: the systematic training of a Galilean Jewish home, the Nazareth synagogue school, and contact with the caravans and with nature. Above all, his real education came through close association with people, and The Urantia Book says that "⟦Q 123:5.8⟧Jesus era altamente educado, no sentido em que, aos humanos, ele os entendia profundamente e os amava com devoção.⟦/Q⟧" [123:5.8].

Around the time this education began, on February 11, 2 B.C., when Jesus was a little under five years of age, the Thought Adjuster came to indwell him, and like every other child he did not know of the arrival of this divine monitor [123:2.1].

1. Home Education: A School of Questions and Answers

The most valuable part of Jesus' early education was the answers he received from his parents to his thoughtful and searching inquiries [123:2.3]. "⟦Q 123:2.3⟧Desde o momento em que Jesus tinha cinco anos de idade até ter dez anos, ele foi um ponto de interrogação contínuo.⟦/Q⟧" [123:2.3]. The Galilean Jews divided a child's life into seven stages; until the fifth birthday the mother was responsible for education, and after that a boy was taught by his father, so on August 21, 2 B.C., Mary formally handed him over to Joseph [123:2.5, 123:2.13]. His mother taught him to care for the vines and flowers of the garden and had him practice drawing maps and writing Aramaic, Greek, and Hebrew in the sandbox on the roof, and he became fluent in all three languages [123:2.14].

2. The Synagogue School: The Law and the Prophets

At seven he entered the synagogue school of Nazareth; for three years he learned the rudiments of the law in Hebrew, and for the next three years he studied the deeper teachings of the law, memorizing them by repeating them aloud; at thirteen he graduated and became a "⟦Q 123:5.2⟧son of the commandment⟦/Q⟧" [123:5.1, 123:5.2]. The pupils sat in a semicircle facing the teacher, the chazan, and studied the law from Leviticus onward, then the prophets and the Psalms; there were no textbooks, and the pupils repeated the chazan's words in unison [123:5.3, 123:5.5]. On entering school he chose as his "birthday text" the passage from Isaiah that begins "⟦Q 123:5.11⟧The spirit of the Lord God is upon me⟦/Q⟧" [123:5.11]. Toward his graduation the chazan told Joseph that he feared he had learned more from Jesus' searching questions than he had been able to teach the lad [123:5.9].

3. The Caravans and the Synagogue Lectures: Windows on the World

Nazareth was a caravan way station and crossroads, most of its population was gentile, and it was the place in Galilee where the traditional law was most liberally interpreted [123:5.7]. Jesus learned about human nature by talking freely in Greek with people of many nations who came to his father's repair shop and with caravan travelers at the spring [123:5.6]. And every Sabbath he heard the lectures of distinguished visitors and became acquainted with the views of many thinkers of the Jewish world [123:5.10].

4. Nature and Work with the Hands

On Sabbath afternoons Joseph would take him up the hills and show him Mount Carmel, Mount Hermon, the Jordan valley, and the Mediterranean, telling him the stories of Elijah and the prophets [123:5.12]. Apart from the instruction at the fireside, Jesus' earliest training had to do with a reverent and sympathetic contact with nature [123:5.14]. He learned to milk the cow, care for the animals, make cheese, and weave, and at ten he was an expert loom operator [123:5.15].

Summary

Jesus received his moral training and spiritual culture chiefly at home, his intellectual and theological education chiefly from the chazan, and his real education, preparing him for the tests of life, through association with his fellows [123:5.8]. This story reminds us that parents who value questions, learning amid nature and work, and the capacity to understand and love people are the heart of true education [123:2.3, 123:5.14].

q290.question: What does the event at age thirteen, when Jesus discussed with the teachers in the Jerusalem temple and spoke to his parents of his "Father's business," show us?
q290.answer:
Having finished the synagogue school at thirteen and become a "⟦Q 123:5.2⟧son of the commandment⟦/Q⟧," Jesus attended the Passover at Jerusalem with his parents for the first time [123:5.2]. This visit was the event in which he first began to be clearly conscious of his life mission, and it was also the moment when his lifelong attitude of harmonizing devotion to his heavenly Father with duty to his earthly family first came to light [125:6.11, 125:6.12].

1. The Shock He Received in the Temple

Jesus was shocked by the spirit of irreverence he witnessed in the temple courts. The court of the gentiles was full of the noise of the money-changers and the merchants of sacrificial animals, and the sight of courtesans parading within the temple precincts aroused his youthful indignation [125:1.1, 125:1.2]. He admired the sentiment and service of the temple, but "⟦Q 125:1.3⟧he was shocked by the spiritual ugliness which he beheld on the faces of so many of the unthinking worshipers⟦/Q⟧" [125:1.3]. The bloody spectacle of animals being slaughtered before the altar was more than this nature-loving boy could bear [125:1.4].

2. A Discussion in Which He Taught by Asking Questions

Even after his parents had left for home, Jesus remained in the temple and took part in the discussions of the scribes and teachers, and by the third day the whole attention of the chief discussion group of the temple was focused on his questions [125:5.1, 125:5.2]. He asked what was really in the holy of holies behind the veil, why mothers should be segregated from the male worshipers, why, if God is a loving Father, so many animals must be slaughtered, whether it was right to permit trading in the temple, and whether the Messiah was to be a temporal prince sitting on David's throne or the light of a spiritual kingdom [125:5.3-5.7]. He conveyed his teaching through the questions he asked and showed an attitude of never taking unfair advantage of others, an attitude that later characterized his whole public ministry [125:5.8]. He was free from any desire to win an argument and was concerned only with proclaiming truth and more fully revealing God [125:5.8].

3. The Answer: "My Father's Business"

Mary, who had searched for her son for more than three days, rebuked him in front of everyone, and so one of the greatest opportunities ever to come to him came to an inglorious end [125:6.5, 125:6.6]. After a moment's thought Jesus answered: "⟦Q 125:6.7⟧Não devias esperar encontrar-me na casa do meu Pai, já que é chegado o momento em que devo cuidar dos assuntos do meu Pai?”⟦/Q⟧" [125:6.7] Then, relieving his parents' embarrassment, he said that no one had done anything except what he thought best, and suggested that they go home [125:6.8]. On the way back, on the brow of the Mount of Olives, he lamented that Jerusalem had become a victim of the Roman yoke and of its own traditions, and exclaimed that he would return and cleanse the temple [125:6.9].

4. Between the Heavenly Father and the Earthly Father

On reaching home Jesus assured his parents of his affection and said: "⟦Q 125:6.11⟧“Embora eu deva cumprir a vontade do meu Pai no céu, eu serei também obediente ao meu pai na Terra. Aguardarei a minha hora”.⟦/Q⟧." [125:6.11] Even when in his mind he did not consent to his parents' misguided plans, he gracefully conformed to the customs of his family in every way consistent with his dedication to doing the Father's will, and The Urantia Book judges that he was "an artist" in adjusting his dedication to duty to the obligations of family loyalty and social service [125:6.12].

5. Differing Interpretations

Joseph was perplexed, but Mary took the words spoken on the Mount of Olives as a prediction of his Messianic mission as the deliverer of Israel. And she began with new energy to try to mold his thinking along patriotic and nationalistic lines [125:6.13]. This misunderstanding later led to tension between Jesus and his family.

Summary

The temple episode was the event in which Jesus first showed a deep critical awareness of formal and irreverent worship, and first revealed the gifts of a teacher who awakens truth by asking questions [125:1.3, 125:5.8]. He had become aware of his "Father's business," yet he did not hurry; he chose to obey his earthly parents and await his hour [125:6.11]. This teaches that even one who has received a high calling must faithfully carry out his present duties.

q291.question: How did the adolescent Jesus come to terms with the Jewish Messianic expectations and his own mission, and why did he choose the title "Son of Man"?
q291.answer:
Jesus did not live knowing from the start everything about who he was and what he had come to do; rather, during his adolescence he worked it out through a long struggle among the Scriptures, his family's expectations, and his own inner convictions. In particular, in his fifteenth year, when he had become head of the family after his father Joseph's death, he went through much difficulty with confused thinking, and during this period he arrived at the firm conviction that he was not the kind of Messiah the Jews expected, and also adopted the title "Son of Man" [126:3.5, 126:3.6, 126:3.8].

1. Conflicting Expectations within the Family

From the beginning Jesus' parents held differing expectations. On the way to Bethlehem Joseph clung firmly to the idea of a spiritual teacher, while Mary held to the concept of the Jewish Messiah as the deliverer of the Hebrew nation [122:7.5]. After the temple episode Mary devoted herself to preparing him to be a leader who would restore the throne of David [125:6.13]. Jesus' confusion grew up in the midst of these two currents.

2. The Conclusion That He Was Not That Kind of Messiah

He thoroughly considered the Jewish idea of the Messiah and became firmly convinced that he was not that Messiah. He did not expect to lead a Jewish army to overthrow foreign domination, he knew he would never sit on the throne of David, and he did not think his mission was for the Jews alone [126:3.6]. Yet even after he had settled that the essence of his mission was "his Father's business," the revealing of the Father's loving nature to all mankind, the Scripture passages about the deliverer, his mother's insistence, and questions about his relations to his family, to Judaism, to Rome, and to the gentiles continued to trouble him [126:3.10, 126:3.11].

3. The "Son of Man" Found in the Book of Enoch

While pondering these problems, he found in the synagogue library at Nazareth a manuscript called "⟦Q 126:3.8⟧The Book of Enoch⟦/Q⟧." He was certain that it had not been written by Enoch of old, but he was deeply impressed by the passage telling how the Son of Man had walked through the courts of heavenly glory with the Father and then turned his back on that glory to come down and proclaim salvation to needy mortals [126:3.8]. Although he knew that much of the Eastern mysticism mixed into that book was erroneous, he recognized that of all the Messianic predictions and theories about the deliverer none was so near the truth as this story, and he decided to adopt "⟦Q 126:3.8⟧the Son of Man⟦/Q⟧" as his inaugural title [126:3.8]. The Urantia Book adds: "⟦Q 126:3.8⟧Jesus possuía uma inequívoca capacidade de reconhecer a verdade; e jamais hesitou em abraçar a verdade, não importava de que fonte ela emanasse.⟦/Q⟧." [126:3.8]

4. His First Sermon in the Synagogue and the Lord's Prayer

On the first Sabbath after his fifteenth birthday he conducted the morning service of the Nazareth synagogue, reading the passage from Isaiah beginning "⟦Q 126:4.2⟧The spirit of the Lord God is upon me⟦/Q⟧" and other words of the prophets [126:4.1, 126:4.2]. His choice of texts, speaking of liberation and comfort, of justice and mercy, and of God's care, shows the character of the mission he envisioned [126:4.5, 126:4.6]. In the same year, while trying to teach his younger brothers and sisters to pray individually, he first formulated the family prayer that would later become known as the "Lord's Prayer" [126:3.3, 126:3.4].

5. Learning to Carry His Burdens Alone

From this year on Jesus learned not to disclose all his thoughts, not even to his mother, and although outwardly he became commonplace, he longed for a friend who could understand his problems [126:3.14]. "⟦Q 126:3.14⟧A singularidade dessa situação excepcional compeliu-o a carregar o seu fardo sozinho.⟦/Q⟧" [126:3.14]. He did not tell these decisions to his mother, who still held to the idea of his being the Messiah [126:3.9].

Summary

The adolescent Jesus rejected the image of a political Messiah, settled that the essence of his mission was to reveal the Father's love to all mankind, and, having found in the Book of Enoch a picture close to the truth, chose "⟦Q 126:3.6⟧the Son of Man⟦/Q⟧" as his title [126:3.6, 126:3.8, 126:3.10]. This working out was finally completed later in the decisions of the forty days [136:9.8].

q292.question: Why did Jesus not marry, and how did he respond to the love of Rebecca, the daughter of Ezra?
q292.answer:
The Urantia Book shows that there were two levels of reasons why Jesus did not marry. One was the universe directive he had received before his bestowal; the other was his human duty to support the family that had lost its father. And the issue actually came into his life through the love of Rebecca, the daughter of Ezra, a wealthy merchant of Nazareth [127:5.1].

1. The Pre-bestowal Directive: Leaving No Offspring

Immanuel told Michael that he would live the normal social life of the planet but would probably not enter the marriage relation. Marriage "⟦Q 120:3.8⟧would be wholly honorable and consistent with your bestowal⟦/Q⟧," but one of the incarnation mandates of Sonarington forbids a bestowal Son of Paradise origin to leave human offspring behind on a planet [120:3.8]. Jesus' celibacy, therefore, was not a low estimate of marriage but a result of his special status as a bestowal Son.

2. Rebecca's Love and Her Family's Response

Although poor, Jesus was one of the most outstanding young men of Nazareth, a fine specimen of robust and intelligent manhood [127:5.1]. Rebecca first confided in Miriam, and Mary and Miriam tried to dissuade her by telling her of their belief that Jesus was a son of destiny, but Rebecca thought that such a man needed a faithful wife all the more [127:5.1, 127:5.2]. Her father invited Jesus to Rebecca's seventeenth birthday celebration, intending to make good the family's loss of income if Jesus married [127:5.2].

3. The Sacred Duty of Supporting His Family

Jesus replied kindly that no amount of money could take the place of his personal obligation to rear his father's family, the obligation to "⟦Q 127:5.3⟧fulfill the most sacred of all human trusts—loyalty to one's own flesh and blood⟦/Q⟧" [127:5.3]. Moved by these words, Ezra said to his wife: "⟦Q 127:5.3⟧“Não poderemos tê-lo como filho; ele é nobre demais para nós”.⟦/Q⟧." [127:5.3]

4. His Answer to Rebecca

This conversation was a real test for Jesus as well. Until then he had never seriously considered the consummation of personal love in marriage, but now he faced a problem that every average human being must confront, and indeed was he "⟦Q 127:5.4⟧tested in all points like as you are⟦/Q⟧" [127:5.4]. He sincerely thanked Rebecca for her admiration, saying that it would cheer and comfort him all the days of his life, but explained that he was not free to enter into relations with any woman other than those of simple brotherly regard and pure friendship [127:5.5]. He added that he could not consider marriage until his family was reared, and: "⟦Q 127:5.5⟧“Se sou um filho predestinado, não devo assumir obrigações que durem toda uma vida; até o momento em que o meu destino se torne manifestado”.⟦/Q⟧" [127:5.5].

5. Rebecca's Later Life

Heartbroken, Rebecca moved with her family to Sepphoris, refused every man who sought her hand, and waited for the time when he would begin his career as a teacher of truth [127:5.6]. She followed him devotedly through the years of his public labors; she was present, unnoticed by Jesus, on the day of his entry into Jerusalem, and she stood "⟦Q 127:5.6⟧among the other women⟦/Q⟧" beside Mary on the tragic afternoon when the Son of Man hung upon the cross [127:5.6]. To her, as well as to countless worlds on high, he was "⟦Q 127:5.6⟧the one altogether lovely and the greatest among ten thousand⟦/Q⟧" [127:5.6]. This brief story shows that Jesus' refusal was not coldness but a form of love grounded in mutual respect.

Summary

Jesus did not marry because of the universe mandate that a bestowal Son leave no offspring on a planet, and because of his human responsibility to support to the end the family that had lost its father [120:3.8, 127:5.3, 127:5.5]. He did not take love lightly; while courteously respecting Rebecca's heart, he put his duty first. This episode shows how to choose honestly and kindly when faced with a conflict between love and responsibility.

q293.question: Why did Jesus decline the offer to head the school at Damascus, and why did he keep the various periods of his life separate from one another?
q293.answer:
During the last four months of his twenty-third year, Jesus stayed at the home of a merchant in Damascus and was offered the headship of a school of religious philosophy that was to outrival Alexandria. The Urantia Book presents this as "⟦Q 128:4.1⟧one of the greatest temptations that Jesus ever faced in the course of his purely human career⟦/Q⟧" [128:4.1]. He declined the offer, and he did not tell even his family about it [128:4.4].

1. The Offer at Damascus

This merchant, who was part Jewish, offered to devote an extraordinary sum of money and proposed that Jesus make a tour of the world's educational centers in preparation for becoming its head [128:4.1]. He brought before Jesus twelve merchants and bankers who had agreed to support the school; Jesus helped them plan its organization, but he always expressed the fear that his unstated prior obligations would prevent him from accepting its direction [128:4.2]. The merchant persistently tried to persuade him, but Jesus would not consent.

2. The Reason for Declining: Not to Be Bound by the "Councils of Men"

Jesus well knew that his mission on earth was not to be supported by institutions of learning, and that he must not obligate himself in the least to be directed by the "councils of men," no matter how well-intentioned [128:4.2]. This also corresponds to the advice he had received before his bestowal, the directive to avoid the formation of an organized cult or a crystallized religion [120:3.6]. Ironically, the one who was rejected by the religious leaders of Jerusalem was acclaimed as a brilliant teacher by the businessmen of Damascus when he was an unknown carpenter [128:4.3].

3. Deliberately Separating the Periods of His Life

Very cleverly and deliberately, Jesus kept the various episodes of his life separate so that the world would not connect them as the doings of one individual [128:4.5]. The people of Damascus never connected the teacher of Capernaum, who later stirred up Jewish society, with the Nazareth carpenter who had declined their school [128:4.4]. On his Mediterranean tour, too, he was known as "the Damascus scribe" or "the Jewish tutor," and no one except Zebedee knew he had made that journey [129:3.2, 129:3.3, 129:3.4].

4. The Intent to Prevent a Religion That Exalts the Teacher

The purpose was to prevent the building up of a spectacular career that would cause later generations to venerate the teacher instead of obeying the truth he had lived and taught [128:4.6]. Very early he recognized that his followers would be tempted to formulate a "religion about him" which might become a competitor of the gospel of the kingdom he intended to proclaim [128:4.6]. Accordingly he consistently suppressed anything that might be made to serve "⟦Q 128:4.6⟧this natural human tendency to exalt the teacher in place of proclaiming his teachings⟦/Q⟧" [128:4.6].

5. Respect That Refused Undue Influence

From the same motive he allowed himself to be known by various titles during different periods of his life [128:4.7]. He did not want to exert undue influence on his family or others that would lead them to believe in him against their honest convictions, and he did not want people to believe in him unless their hearts responded to the spiritual realities revealed in his teachings [128:4.7]. The Urantia Book says that to understand many of Jesus' strange doings we must always keep in mind the motive of the bestowal: he was careful not to build up an overattractive and attention-consuming career [129:3.5].

Summary

Jesus declined the honor at Damascus so that his mission would not be bound to human institutions and patrons, and he deliberately separated the periods of his life so that people would not miss the truth by worshiping the teacher [128:4.2, 128:4.5, 128:4.6]. This shows his humility and his respect for others, desiring that the truth itself, rather than personal fame, should reach people's hearts [128:4.7].

q294.question: Did Jesus live as an example that everyone must copy exactly? What does the life of "Jesus the man" mean for us?
q294.answer:
The Urantia Book's answer is clear. Jesus did not live in order to set an example for all people of all ages to imitate in every detail. He lived a true and genuinely human life, and therefore we draw much inspiration from his life, but the example he set was not of living the same life but of living in the same way and by the same means [129:4.7].

1. Not an Example to Be Copied

The Urantia Book says: "⟦Q 129:4.7⟧Jesus não viveu a sua vida na Terra com o fito de estabelecer um exemplo para todos os outros seres humanos copiarem.⟦/Q⟧." [129:4.7] He did not come to be a perfect and detailed example for any child or adult, man or woman, of that age or any other [129:4.7]. This also agrees with Immanuel's pre-bestowal instructions: his earth life was not to be lived as an example for the Urantians of his day or of later generations, but rather as an inspiration for all life on all worlds [120:2.7]. Furthermore, he was incarnated in the mind of a first-century human being and was shaped by the heredity, environment, and education of his time, so his humanity was a real humanity formed under the conditions of that age [136:8.7].

2. The Way of Living in the Same Manner

What, then, should we follow? Just as Jesus lived his mortal life in his day and as he was, he set the example for us to live in our day and as we are [129:4.7]. The Urantia Book says: "⟦Q 129:4.7⟧Vós podeis não aspirar viver a vida dele, mas podeis resolver viver as vossas vidas como ele viveu a dele e pelos mesmos meios.⟦/Q⟧." [129:4.7] That way and those means were trust in and submission to the Father's will and communion with the indwelling spirit. During this period, although he did not appear to engage in many seasons of formal communion, he perfected increasingly effective methods of personal communication with the indwelling spirit presence of the Father [129:4.3].

3. One Who Knows the Whole of Human Experience

Jesus lived a real, full, and truly normal and average life in the flesh [129:4.3]. He experienced human emotions ranging from superb joy to profound sorrow; he was a child of joy and a being of rare good humor, and at the same time a "⟦Q 129:4.4⟧man of sorrows and acquainted with grief⟦/Q⟧" [129:4.4]. He not only lived the human life from infancy to death but fully experienced the stage of human and Adjuster reconciliation, which Urantia mortals rarely attain [129:4.5]. Therefore he knows our thoughts and feelings, our desires and impulses.

4. A Revelation to Both God and Man

His life did not receive the universal approval of his contemporaries, but it was fully and unqualifiedly accepted by the Universal Father. In one and the same personality-life it accomplished at once the full revelation of the eternal God to man and the presentation of perfected human personality to the satisfaction of the Infinite Creator [129:4.6]. By the end of his twenty-ninth year he, who had come as the fullness of God to be manifest to man, had become well-nigh the perfection of man to be manifest to God [129:4.8].

5. The New and Living Way

Jesus may not be the technical and detailed example for the mortals of all the realms of this local universe, but he is everlastingly the inspiration and guide of all pilgrims on their way to Havona and Paradise [129:4.7]. The Urantia Book calls him this: "⟦Q 129:4.7⟧Jesus é o caminho novo e vivo do homem até Deus, do parcial ao perfeito, do terreno ao celeste, do tempo para a eternidade.⟦/Q⟧." [129:4.7]

Summary

Jesus is not a model whose outward appearance we are to duplicate, but the one who opened the way for each of us to live trusting the Father in our own time and our own circumstances [129:4.7]. He knows the whole of human experience [129:4.5], he revealed both God and man [129:4.6], and his life becomes our example only when we live by the same way of faith.

q295.question: How did Jesus help the people he met personally during his Mediterranean tour, and what were the characteristics of that personal ministry?
q295.answer:
Before beginning his public ministry, from April of A.D. 22 to December of A.D. 23, Jesus traveled through the Roman world with Gonod of India and his son Ganid [130:0.1]. He spent about half of each day teaching Ganid and serving as Gonod's interpreter, and devoted the rest of his time to intimate personal contact with people [130:0.5]. To celestial observers this tour was the most fascinating of all his earth experiences, because it was the period of his "personal ministry," carried on while he was still one among men [129:4.1].

1. Approaching People Anonymously

Throughout the tour Jesus was known as "the Damascus scribe" or "the Jewish tutor," and no one except Zebedee knew that he had made this journey [129:3.2, 129:3.3]. Most of the people he helped never learned that the strange teacher was the Jesus of whom they later heard [130:8.1, 133:9.5]. His interest was not in fame but in people themselves.

2. The Wisdom That Opens Hearts: The Young Man of Crete

In the mountains of Crete he met a young man gripped by fear and a sense of inferiority. First he asked him the way to Phoenix, letting the youth gladly help him, and then said that he would now show him the way to the city of his frustrated hopes [130:6.2]. He reminded the young man of his strong body and clear mind and, above all, of "⟦Q 130:6.3⟧the spirit which lives within you⟦/Q⟧," and encouraged him that his mind should be not the slave of fear but his ally in solving life's problems [130:6.3]. And he said: "⟦Q 130:6.4⟧This day, my son, you are to be reborn⟦/Q⟧" [130:6.4]. This young man, Fortune, later became the leader of the Christians in Crete [130:6.5]. In Malta, too, he helped Claudus, who had contemplated taking his life, resolve to face life like a man [130:8.1].

3. Questions and Listening, and Immediately Helpful Advice

During the six months in Rome he came into affectionate contact with upward of five hundred people [132:4.3]. He usually drew people into conversation by asking questions, and to those he taught the most, he said the least [132:4.2]. Especially the overburdened, anxious, and dejected gained much relief by unburdening their souls to a sympathetic listener, and he was always able to offer practical and immediately helpful suggestions for correcting their real difficulties, while conveying the love of God [132:4.2]. The burden of his message was always the heavenly Father's love and mercy, together with the good news that man is a faith-son of God [132:4.2].

4. Words Suited to Each Person's Situation

He met people of every walk of life: a senator, a slaveholder, a physician, a soldier, an orator, and others. The slaveholder Claudius freed one hundred and seventeen slaves the day after spending an evening with him, and a Greek physician came to see his patients as beings with minds and souls as well as bodies [132:4.5]. To a Roman soldier he said: "⟦Q 132:4.6⟧“Que o teu coração seja tão valente quanto o teu punho.⟦/Q⟧." [132:4.6] And for a poor man who had been falsely accused, he pleaded before the magistrate and secured his release [132:4.8].

5. Distinguishing Mercy from Justice

Near Tarentum he seized a bully who was attacking a weaker boy and let the boy escape, but when Ganid wanted to beat the bully, he stopped him [133:1.1]. He explained: "⟦Q 133:1.2⟧Mercy ministry is always the work of the individual, but justice punishment is the function of the social, governmental, or universe administrative groups⟦/Q⟧." [133:1.2] The individual is to show mercy, while punishment should be left to fair judgment by those who fully know the motives [133:1.2].

Summary

The personal ministry of the Mediterranean tour was characterized by anonymity, the wisdom that opens hearts, listening and asking questions, practical help, and always the proclamation of the fatherhood of God [129:3.3, 130:6.2, 132:4.2]. Jesus regarded this period as one of the richest and most informative of his earth life [132:4.3].

q296.question: What kind of faith was "our religion," which Ganid formulated himself after collecting the world's religions?
q296.answer:
During the sojourn at Alexandria, the young Ganid spent no small sum of his father's money employing more than threescore translators to collect what the world's religions teach about God and his relations with man [131:0.1]. He arranged this material under ten heads, and finally he set down the belief he had reached as a result of Jesus' teaching, which he called "our religion" [131:0.2, 131:10.1]. This record was preserved in India for hundreds of years after his death [131:0.2].

The Urantia Book makes plain that the monotheistic teachings contained in this collection were largely derived from the preachments of the Salem missionaries of Machiventa Melchizedek [131:0.1]. On that foundation, "our religion" expresses, as the confession of a young man, the concept of God that he learned from Jesus.

1. One God, the Loving Heavenly Father

Ganid's confession begins with "⟦Q 131:10.2⟧The Lord our God is one Lord⟦/Q⟧" and says that we should love him with all our mind and heart and love all his children as ourselves [131:10.2]. This one God is our heavenly Father, in whom all things consist, and his spirit dwells in every sincere human soul [131:10.2]. Though we cannot see God, we can know him, and by daily living the Father's will we can reveal him to our fellows [131:10.2].

2. God Known Not by Knowledge but by Experience

He confesses: "⟦Q 131:10.3⟧Nós não podemos procurar a Deus pelo conhecimento, mas podemos conhecê-lo nos nossos corações pela experiência pessoal.⟦/Q⟧." [131:10.3] Though God's justice may be past finding out, his mercy may be received by the humblest being, and while the Father fills the universe, he also lives in our hearts [131:10.3]. The Father will not let any child who longs to find him and be like him perish, and he loves even the wicked and is kind to the unthankful [131:10.4].

3. From "Father of All" to "My Father"

The key turn in this confession is the personal decision not to rest in the belief that God is the Father of all people but to say, "⟦Q 131:10.5⟧I will henceforth believe that he is also my Father⟦/Q⟧" [131:10.5]. He says that first of all he will practice worship by learning to do God's will on earth, that is, by treating each of his fellows just as he thinks God would like to have him treated [131:10.5]. And he confesses that, best of all, God is his spirit Father, and that he is sometime going forth to see him [131:10.6].

4. The Union of Fatherhood and Brotherhood

Ganid says he has learned that man may become a son of God, and that the fact that all men are his brothers sometimes even terrifies him, but that it must be true [131:10.7]. He confesses: "⟦Q 131:10.7⟧Não vejo como posso rejubilar com a paternidade de Deus enquanto recusar a aceitar a irmandade dos homens.⟦/Q⟧." [131:10.7] Therefore he resolves to do his good deeds in secret, to pray most when by himself, to judge not, and to learn to love his enemies [131:10.8].

5. His Conclusion in Comparison with Other Religions

He concludes that although he sees God in other religions too, the God of "our religion" is more beautiful, loving, merciful, personal, and positive [131:10.8]. He says that this new religion is very full of joy and generates an enduring happiness [131:10.6]. After returning to India, Ganid became an influential man and spread abroad many of the truths he had learned from Jesus [133:9.5].

Summary

"Our religion" can be summed up as one heavenly Father, a God known by experience, the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, and worship lived out in the service of one's fellows [131:10.2, 131:10.3, 131:10.5, 131:10.7]. It shows that the heart of Jesus' teaching is a faith that respects the truth in many religions while meeting God personally as "my Father."

q297.question: What principles of religious sovereignty and political sovereignty did Jesus teach in the Urmia lectures?
q297.answer:
In A.D. 24, during a caravan trip to the Caspian Sea, Jesus stopped at Urmia in Persia. On one of the islands there stood a temple of the philosophy of religions built by the wealthy merchant Cymboyton and his three sons, where teachers of more than thirty religions taught and debated together [134:3.1, 134:3.2, 134:3.6]. On his return trip Jesus delivered twenty-four lectures here on "⟦Q 134:3.5⟧the brotherhood of men⟦/Q⟧," and "⟦Q 134:3.5⟧Esses foram os mais sistemáticos e formais de todos os ensinamentos do Mestre em Urântia.⟦/Q⟧" [134:3.5]. In reality their subject was the "Kingdom of God" and the "Kingdoms of Men" [134:3.5].

One point calls for caution. The midwayers state that they restated these teachings as applied to twentieth-century conditions. A disagreement arose between the seraphim of the churches and the seraphim of progress, and in the end the Melchizedek chairman appointed three midwayers, whose restatement adapted to modern times was edited and included [134:3.8]. They add that the section on political sovereignty in particular departs more widely from the Master's original teaching [134:5.1].

1. Brotherhood Founded on the Fatherhood of God

The starting point of the lectures is that "⟦Q 134:4.1⟧A irmandade dos homens é fundada na paternidade de Deus.⟦/Q⟧." [134:4.1] The kingdom of heaven is founded on divine sovereignty, and since God is spirit, it is a spiritual relationship between God and man [134:4.2]. God gives a fragment of his spirit to each person, so spiritually all men are equal, and in the kingdom of heaven there are no castes, classes, or economic groups [134:4.7].

2. The Condition of Religious Peace: God Alone Is Spirit Sovereign

Intolerance and persecution arise when a religion assumes that it is superior to all others and claims exclusive authority [134:4.3]. Religious peace is possible only when all religions give up all concepts of ecclesiastical authority and spiritual sovereignty, for "⟦Q 134:4.4⟧Apenas Deus é soberano em espírito.⟦/Q⟧" [134:4.4]. The kingdom of heaven in men's hearts produces religious unity, not uniformity [134:4.6]. The teachers at Urmia lived in peace precisely because they had completely given up the concept of religious sovereignty [134:4.10].

3. The Evolution of Political Sovereignty

War will not end so long as nations cling to the concept of unlimited national sovereignty; the only true levels of relative sovereignty are the spiritual free will of the individual and the collective sovereignty of mankind as a whole [134:5.2]. Political sovereignty has evolved through organization from the family to the clan, the tribe, the nation, and the empire [134:5.6], and as sovereignty passes to larger groups, small wars decrease but the potential for great wars increases [134:5.7]. Therefore, it says, peace will not come until the nations surrender the power to make war to a government representing all mankind [134:5.12]. The forty-eight American states, which ceased fighting one another by surrendering their sovereignty to the federal union, are given as an example [134:5.13, 134:5.14].

4. Law and Liberty

A group of liberty-loving people cannot live in peace without submitting to a law that guarantees equal liberty to all [134:6.1]. Religion makes brotherhood spiritually possible, but a government of mankind is needed to regulate social, economic, and political problems [134:6.2]. "⟦Q 134:6.7⟧A guerra não é a grande e terrível doença do homem; a guerra é um sintoma, um resultado. A doença, de fato, é o vírus da soberania nacional.⟦/Q⟧." [134:6.7] Individuals, it says, would enjoy even greater liberty under a world government [134:6.10].

5. The End of the Urmia School

After Cymboyton's death the school encountered difficulties, and when the Christian teachers who later joined tried to place their religion above other beliefs, confusion increased until the school finally closed [134:6.14, 134:6.15, 134:6.16]. This ending paradoxically confirms the lesson of the lectures.

Summary

The Urmia lectures taught brotherhood founded on the fatherhood of God, the principle of religious peace that God alone is spirit sovereign, and a political peace possible only under the sovereignty of mankind as a whole [134:4.1, 134:4.4, 134:6.13]. It must be remembered, however, that the present text is a restatement by the midwayers adapted to twentieth-century conditions [134:3.8, 134:5.1].

q298.question: What was the "great temptation" that Jesus underwent on Mount Hermon, and how does it differ from the Gospel story of the temptation in the wilderness?
q298.answer:
According to The Urantia Book, Jesus' real "great temptation" took place not in the wilderness after his baptism but on Mount Hermon in the late summer of A.D. 25, some months before his baptism [134:8.4, 134:8.9]. It was not a test involving bread, the temple pinnacle, or the kingdoms of the world, but a confrontation with Satan, representing Lucifer, and Caligastia, the rebellious Planetary Prince; it "⟦Q 134:8.6⟧had not to do with the kingdoms of this world but with the sovereignty of a mighty and glorious universe⟦/Q⟧" [134:8.6].

1. The Sojourn on the Mountain, Undertaken Alone

Jesus spent the last three weeks of August and the first three weeks of September on Mount Hermon [134:8.4]. He asked the Father that even his guardian seraphim be sent away, went alone into the final struggle of mortal existence, and relied only on his indwelling Thought Adjuster [134:8.2]. During this time he finished the mortal task of attaining the circles of mind-understanding and personality-control, and became fully convinced that his divine nature was superior to his human nature [134:8.4, 134:8.5].

2. A Confrontation with Real Beings

The superhuman beings he faced on the mountain were not the hallucinations of a starving man but real beings, his archenemies of the system of Satania [134:8.3]. In the last week of the sojourn he asked permission to hold conference with his Satania enemies as the Son of Man, as Joshua ben Joseph, and Satan and Caligastia were made fully visible to him [134:8.6]. This was the fulfillment of the task Immanuel had recommended before the bestowal: to bring the rebellion to an end in the likeness of the lowest of his creatures [120:2.2].

3. A Single Answer

To all the proposals and compromises offered by Lucifer's emissaries, Jesus only replied, "⟦Q 134:8.8⟧The will of my Father in Paradise be done⟦/Q⟧." [134:8.8] Saying that as their Creator-father he could hardly judge them fairly, he referred them to the judgment of the higher courts of the universe, the Ancients of Days [134:8.7]. When the ordeal was finished, the guardian seraphim returned and ministered to him [134:8.8].

4. The Result: The Attainment of Sovereignty and the Settlement of the Rebellion

On an afternoon in late summer, amid the quiet of the woods, Michael of Nebadon attained the unquestioned sovereignty of his universe [134:8.9]. The universal announcement came months later, on the day of his baptism, but in reality it was accomplished that day on the mountain, and when he came down from the mountain, the Lucifer rebellion and the Caligastia secession were virtually settled [134:8.9]. On that day Jesus of Nazareth became, on the universe records, the Planetary Prince of Urantia [136:3.1]. Coming down from the mountain he said to Tiglath: "⟦Q 134:8.10⟧The period of rest is over; I must return to my Father's business⟦/Q⟧." [134:8.10]

5. The Difference from the Wilderness Temptation Story

The Urantia Book says: "⟦Q 134:8.6⟧O simbolismo, nas vossas escrituras, foi elaborado para ser dirigido a épocas anteriores, nas quais o pensamento do mundo ainda era infantil.⟦/Q⟧" [134:8.6]. The forty days after the baptism were not a period of temptation but the "period of great decisions" in which he planned his public ministry; later this retreat was confused with the struggles on Mount Hermon and, because of the tradition that great leaders fast before their ministry, it was symbolically combined with the temptation story [136:4.10]. In fact he did not fast for forty days, and during that period he was not tempted by any evil spirits or rebel beings [136:4.3]. The so-called great temptation therefore took place not right after the baptism but before it [134:8.9].

Summary

The great temptation on Mount Hermon was the event in which the Son of Man rejected, solely through trust in the Father's will, the compromises that Satan and Caligastia offered concerning universe sovereignty [134:8.6, 134:8.8]. Through it Michael attained his sovereignty and virtually settled the rebellion, and the Gospel story of the temptation in the wilderness is a symbolic merging of this event with the forty-day period of decision [134:8.9, 136:4.10].

q299.question: How did the message of John the Baptist differ from that of Jesus, and how did John understand Jesus?
q299.answer:
John the Baptist and Jesus proclaimed the same "kingdom of heaven," but their emphasis and character differed greatly. The Urantia Book sums it up this way: the burden of John's message was "⟦Q 136:0.2⟧Arrependei-vos, fugi da ira que virá!⟦/Q⟧," whereas in Jesus' preaching the exhortation to repentance was always followed by the gospel, "⟦Q 136:0.2⟧the good tidings of the joy and liberty of the new kingdom⟦/Q⟧" [136:0.2].

1. John: The Last Great Prophet of the Old Order

At fourteen John took the Nazarite vow for life, and following the dress of Elijah he wore a garment of hair and a leather girdle [135:1.1, 135:1.4]. Like Amos he came from the herdsmen, and he thundered his warnings in the "⟦Q 135:6.3⟧spirit and power of Elijah⟦/Q⟧" [135:6.3]. He baptized even Jews in a baptism of repentance "⟦Q 135:6.4⟧for the remission of sins⟦/Q⟧," a new use of the baptism formerly given only to gentile proselytes, and in fifteen months he baptized considerably over one hundred thousand people [135:6.4]. He rebuked the Pharisees and Sadducees who came to be baptized, asking who had warned them, like vipers before the fire, to flee from the wrath to come, and demanded fruits worthy of sincere repentance [135:6.7]; to tax collectors and soldiers he taught concrete justice [135:6.8].

2. John's Concept of the Kingdom: Amid Apocalyptic Expectation

For the Jews of that time, the "kingdom of heaven" meant a righteous state in which God or the Messiah would rule the nations of the earth with perfect power, and the apocalyptists expected the end of Roman rule and the end of the age [135:5.2]. John was very fond of the writings of Daniel, and he never fully rose above the confusion of being unable to reconcile Daniel's "Son of Man" with what his parents had told him about Jesus [135:3.2, 135:3.3]. So the kingdom he proclaimed was taken in many different senses by his hearers, and he solemnly exhorted them to "⟦Q 135:5.8⟧flee from the wrath to come⟦/Q⟧" [135:5.8].

3. Jesus: The Calm and Happy Laborer

The Urantia Book draws the contrast between the two men this way: "⟦Q 136:0.1⟧John was an eager and earnest worker, but Jesus was a calm and happy laborer⟦/Q⟧" [136:0.1]. Jesus was a comfort to the world, but John was hardly a comfort; John preached the kingdom of heaven but hardly entered into the happiness thereof [136:0.1]. Jesus spoke of John as the greatest of the prophets of the old order, but said that the least of those who saw the light of the new way and entered the kingdom was greater than John [136:0.1].

4. Jesus as John Understood Him

Asked whether he was the Messiah, John answered plainly, "I am not," and said that while he baptized with water, one who had been among them would baptize with the Holy Spirit [135:9.4]. He judged that Jesus had come to establish the kingdom of heaven, but exactly what that mission included was never wholly clear in his mind [135:9.5]. After being imprisoned he suffered bitter disappointment and was tempted to doubt because Jesus did not deliver him [135:11.1, 135:11.3]. Yet when his disciples complained of Jesus' prosperity, he answered, "⟦Q 135:11.2⟧He must increase but I must decrease⟦/Q⟧." [135:11.2], confirming that his mission had been to prepare the way.

5. The Final Comfort

A few days before his death John sent messengers to ask, "Are you truly the Messiah?" and Jesus sent word that he had not forgotten him and that the poor were having good tidings preached to them [135:11.4]. This message greatly comforted John and did much to stabilize his faith [135:11.4]. Jesus loved John greatly, but knowing that his earthly work was done, he did not interfere with the natural unfolding of his life [135:11.3].

Summary

John was the last great prophet of the old order, who cried out for judgment and repentance, while Jesus added to repentance the gospel of the heavenly Father's love and the joy of the kingdom [136:0.1, 136:0.2]. John believed in Jesus as the deliverer and prepared the way, but he never fully understood the spiritual nature of that kingdom [135:9.5, 135:11.2]. This contrast shows that, though religion may begin in fear, it must grow into a relationship of joy and liberty.

q300.question: What actually happened at Jesus' baptism, and why did the sinless Jesus receive John's baptism?
q300.answer:
Jesus was baptized by John at noon on Monday, January 14, A.D. 26, in the Jordan near Pella, together with his two brothers James and Jude [135:8.6]. The Urantia Book explains that this baptism was not for repentance or the remission of sins, and that the central event that took place at that time was the return of Jesus' Thought Adjuster in personalized form [136:2.1, 136:2.3].

1. Why He Was Baptized

Not all who received John's baptism received it because of their own personal sins. The Jews believed that the sin of one individual might curse the whole nation, so many devout people were baptized "⟦Q 136:2.1⟧for the good of Israel⟦/Q⟧" [136:2.1]. Hence the text concludes: "⟦Q 136:2.1⟧Evidente é, pois, que Jesus de nenhum modo recebeu o batismo de João como um ritual de arrependimento, nem de remissão de pecados.⟦/Q⟧" [136:2.1]. He was only following the example of many pious Israelites, and he repented of no misdeeds and made no confession of sin. His was a "baptism of consecration" to the doing of the heavenly Father's will [136:2.6].

2. "My Hour Has Come"

When his brothers discussed going to John to be baptized, Jesus, after a night of communion with the Father, laid down his tools in the workshop and said, "⟦Q 135:8.3⟧My hour has come⟦/Q⟧" [135:8.2, 135:8.3]. Recognizing him as he stood in line, John said that he himself ought rather to be baptized, but at Jesus' authoritative tone he baptized him [135:8.5, 135:8.6].

3. The Personalization of the Adjuster

At his baptism Jesus was a mortal who had reached the acme of human evolutionary ascent in mind conquest and self-identification with the spirit, and between his mind and the indwelling Adjuster there was perfect synchrony and full communion [136:2.2]. Ordinarily fusion with the Adjuster follows for a mortal at this stage, and many superhuman observers expected fusion, but "⟦Q 136:2.3⟧Something new and even greater occurred⟦/Q⟧" [136:2.3]. As John laid his hands on him, the Adjuster took leave of the perfected human soul of Joshua ben Joseph and in a few moments returned from Divinington as a Personalized Adjuster, chief of his kind throughout Nebadon [136:2.3].

4. The Heavenly Voice and the Vision

The Personalized Adjuster spoke, saying, "⟦Q 136:2.3⟧This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased⟦/Q⟧" [136:2.3], and these words were spoken on behalf of the Universal Father [136:2.5]. John and the two brothers heard these words, but John's disciples at the water's edge did not, and only Jesus saw the Personalized Adjuster [136:2.3]. In the water Jesus prayed with the first part of what became the Lord's Prayer, and then the heavens were opened and he saw in vision himself as he had been before the incarnation and as he would be afterward [136:2.4]. From then on the Personalized Adjuster was with him in all things for the rest of his earth life [136:2.5].

5. The Meaning of the Baptism: The End of His Human Life and the Beginning of His Public Ministry

The Urantia Book says: "⟦Q 136:2.7⟧Esse dia do batismo pôs fim à vida puramente humana de Jesus.⟦/Q⟧." [136:2.7] The personalization of the Adjuster was the event that attested the completion of the mortal bestowal in the flesh, and at his baptism he heard the final summons to be about his Father's business [136:3.4, 136:2.6]. Afterward he went into seclusion for forty days, following the very procedure that obtains on the morontia worlds when an ascending mortal fuses with the presence of the Father [136:2.6]. The year of the baptism was A.D. 26, the fifteenth year of the actual reign of Tiberius, and he was almost thirty-one and a half years old [136:2.8].

Summary

Jesus' baptism was not for the remission of sins but a baptism of consecration to the Father's will, and at that moment the Adjuster, instead of fusing, returned personalized and acknowledged him in the voice of the Father [136:2.3, 136:2.6]. With this his purely human life ended and his public ministry as the Son of God began [136:2.7].

q301.question: What were the six decisions Jesus made during the forty days after his baptism, and how did they affect his public life?
q301.answer:
After his baptism Jesus withdrew into the Perean hills for forty days. He did not go there to fast or to afflict his soul [136:3.3], but to adjust to his changed relationship with the universe brought about by the personalization of the Adjuster and to settle the policies and methods of his public ministry [136:3.2]. The Urantia Book says that this time was "⟦Q 136:4.10⟧not a period of great temptation but rather the period of the Master's great decisions⟦/Q⟧" [136:4.10]. He made his decisions one by one in lone communion with the Personalized Adjuster, the immediate presence of the Father [136:4.10].

By way of background, Gabriel and the Most High Father of Edentia informed him that his sovereignty had already been recorded and that from then on his course was a matter of his own choice [136:3.5]. He could also choose, according to the situation, between his own way and the Father's way, but he always chose the path of submission to the Father's will [136:4.6-4.9].

1. The First Decision: Not to Use the Celestial Hosts

On the third day he saw the heavenly host, made up of twelve legions of seraphim and representatives of every order of universe intelligence [136:5.1]. He decided not to use any of this host unless the Father's will clearly indicated it, and he placed its command in the hands of the Personalized Adjuster [136:5.2, 136:5.3]. However, functions related to time were not restricted, so that, unless the Father ruled otherwise, all the supernatural elements that appeared in his ministry were associated with the elimination of time [136:5.5].

2. The Second Decision: Not to Use His Power for His Own Needs

In matters of his personal needs he decided to follow the course of normal earthly existence and not to transcend the natural laws he himself had established [136:6.2]. He might use superhuman power for others but never for himself, and he held to this to the very end, when he was mocked on the cross with the words: "⟦Q 136:6.5⟧He saved others; himself he cannot save⟦/Q⟧" [136:6.5]. He was not to be a Messiah who multiplied bread and wine [136:6.8].

3. The Third Decision: Not to Seek Superhuman Protection in Danger

He decided that as a man he would take reasonable precautions but would exclude superhuman intervention even when his life was in danger [136:7.1]. That is why The Urantia Book says that "⟦Q 136:7.3⟧he never walked on the water⟦/Q⟧" [136:7.3] nor did anything that outraged the material order.

4. The Fourth Decision: Not to Attract People by Miracles

He decided not to use universe power to satisfy the craving for signs and wonders [136:8.1]. Miracles stimulate material thinking and produce only outward allegiance; they neither reveal God nor save men [136:8.2]. Instead of the shortcut of walking on the air from the pinnacle of the temple, he chose the natural and patient way of building the kingdom in the hearts of mankind [136:8.5, 136:8.6].

5. The Fifth and Sixth Decisions: Rejecting a Political Messiahship, and Complete Submission

Knowing that the kingdom of heaven is a purely spiritual matter of overthrowing evil in the human heart, he rejected the path of worldly power and of a military Messiah, and he decided to return to Galilee, quietly proclaim the kingdom, and leave the details of procedure to the Father [136:9.2, 136:9.8]. On the last day he declared to the Personalized Adjuster: "⟦Q 136:10.1⟧And in all other matters, as in these now of decision-record, I pledge you I will be subject to the will of my Father⟦/Q⟧." [136:10.1]

The Effect on His Public Life

Because of these decisions he never once wavered in the face of three constantly recurring situations: the clamor to be fed, the insistence on miracles, and the attempt to make him king [136:9.13]. At the same time these choices made certain that the Jews would reject his claims, and so for a long time he sought to prevent his followers from calling him the Messiah [136:9.12].

Summary

The six decisions of the forty days can be summed up as restraint in using the celestial hosts, refusal to use his power for himself, the exclusion of superhuman protection, refusal to attract people by miracles, rejection of a political Messiahship, and the pledge to be subject to the Father's will in all things [136:5.2, 136:6.5, 136:7.1, 136:8.1, 136:9.8, 136:10.1].

q302.question: Was the turning of water into wine at the wedding feast at Cana a miracle? Please explain The Urantia Book's account.
q302.answer:
The Urantia Book explains the story of the wedding feast at Cana in a very distinctive way. The water really did become wine, but it was not a miracle that Jesus intentionally performed, nor was any law of nature broken. The Urantia Book declares, "⟦Q 137:4.13⟧Mas isso, em nenhum sentido, era um milagre.⟦/Q⟧." [137:4.13], and explains that it was an event in which time was eliminated in the presence of the expressed wish of the Universe Creator [137:4.12, 137:4.13].

1. The Atmosphere of the Feast and People's Expectations

Almost a thousand people gathered at the feast, more than four times the number invited, and they showed more interest in welcoming Jesus than in the wedding [137:4.1]. His family and the six disciple-apostles were eagerly expecting him to proclaim the kingdom by some supernatural manifestation [137:4.3]. At this time Jesus was fully self-conscious of his human existence, his divine pre-existence, and the status of his combined natures [137:4.2].

2. Mary's Request and Jesus' Refusal

When Mary asked when he would manifest himself as the supernatural one, Jesus said only: "⟦Q 137:4.4⟧“Se me amais, então estejais dispostos a permanecer comigo, enquanto espero pela vontade do meu Pai que está nos céus”.⟦/Q⟧." [137:4.4] This request was a great disappointment to him, because it proposed that he display divine authority in the very way he had decided against during his isolation in the hills [137:4.5]. He also told his disciples plainly that he had not come to work wonders to satisfy the curious [137:4.6].

3. When the Wine Ran Out

When the wine ran out, Mary again appealed to Jesus, and he replied, "⟦Q 137:4.8⟧We must in all things wait upon the will of the Father in heaven⟦/Q⟧" [137:4.8]. But compassion for his weeping mother moved his human heart, and he began to say that he would gladly do anything within the Father's will, and then stopped [137:4.9]. Mary called to the servants to do whatever he told them, and Jesus realized that he had already said too much, or rather, had wishfully thought too much [137:4.9].

4. What Happened: The Elimination of Time

Seeing the servants drawing wine from the water in six stone jars used for ceremonial purification, Jesus gradually realized what was happening, and on that occasion, "⟦Q 137:4.12⟧De todos aqueles, que estavam presentes à festa de casamento de Caná, Jesus era o mais surpreso.⟦/Q⟧" [137:4.12]. He recalled how the Personalized Adjuster had warned him in the hills that no power could deprive him of the creator prerogative of independence of time [137:4.12]. Since power transformers and midwayers were assembled near the water, the appearance of wine in the presence of the Creator's expressed wish was inescapable, and the Personalized Adjuster signified that this was not contrary to the Father's will [137:4.12]. No law of nature was modified or transcended; nothing happened but the abrogation of time together with the celestial assembly of the chemical elements required for the wine [137:4.13]. This is connected with the fact that, in the first decision of the forty days, the functions related to time alone could not be restricted [136:5.5].

5. Jesus' Reaction and the Lesson

Because of this event people believed in him as the Messiah, but Jesus was sorely perplexed, knowing that they believed in him only because of an unusual occurrence [137:4.16]. He realized that he must be constantly on guard so that sympathy and compassion would not lead to repetitions of such things, yet similar episodes did occur several times afterward [137:4.17].

Summary

The wine at Cana was not a sign Jesus had planned, but an event in which the Creator's independence of time responded to a human wish he cherished in compassion for his mother, so that a natural process took place without time [137:4.12, 137:4.13]. This episode shows that faith that waits upon the Father's will is more precious than faith that leans on miracles [137:4.4, 137:4.16].

q303.question: Through what process were the twelve apostles chosen, and how was the apostolic corps organized and how did it function?
q303.answer:
The twelve apostles were not chosen all at once but in two stages. First Jesus himself chose six men, and then each of those six recommended one more, making twelve [138:1.2, 138:2.2]. The apostles then organized themselves, dividing their roles according to their individual talents [138:10.1].

1. The First Six Apostles: John's Disciples and Galilean Friends

Andrew, a disciple of John the Baptist, was deeply impressed by Jesus and was the first to decide to follow him, and his brother Simon (Peter) joined as well [137:1.1, 137:1.3]. When James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who had been wandering the hills in search of Jesus, asked why he had chosen others first, Jesus calmed their hearts, and they were never envious again [137:1.6, 137:1.7]. From that day the term "apostle" came to distinguish Jesus' chosen family of advisers from the great multitude of believing disciples [137:1.7]. With tears in his eyes, John gave up two of his leading disciples [137:1.8]. On the way to Galilee Jesus said to Philip, "Follow me" [137:2.5], and to Nathaniel, whom Philip brought, he said: "⟦Q 137:2.7⟧Behold a genuine Israelite, in whom there is no deceit. Follow me⟦/Q⟧." [137:2.7]

2. The Six Chosen by the Apostles

In June of A.D. 26 Jesus sent the six apostles out two and two, telling them that he wished to establish twelve apostles to carry on the work of the kingdom after his departure, and that each should choose one man [138:1.1, 138:1.2]. Andrew persuaded his associates that the Master's entrusting this choice to them meant that he trusted them greatly [138:1.3].
