As a result Andrew chose Matthew Levi, Philip chose Thomas, James Zebedee chose James Alpheus, John Zebedee chose Judas Alpheus, Peter chose Simon Zelotes, a high officer of the Zealots, and Nathaniel chose Judas Iscariot, and all were accepted by the unanimous vote of the original six [138:2.2, 138:2.4-2.9].

3. The Organization of the Apostolic Corps

The apostles organized themselves from early on. Andrew, the first chosen, was chairman and director general; Peter, James, and John were Jesus' personal companions; Philip was the steward who provided the food; and Nathaniel looked after the needs of the apostles' families [138:10.2-10.5]. Matthew was the fiscal agent, Thomas the manager of the itinerary, the Alpheus twins handled the multitudes, Simon Zelotes was in charge of recreation and play, and Judas Iscariot was the treasurer who kept the bag [138:10.6-10.10]. This structure was maintained until Judas's defection made a reorganization necessary [138:10.11].

4. Training That Began with a Quiet Personal Ministry

At first Jesus forbade the apostles to baptize or to preach publicly and had them make personal contact with people [138:1.1]. Returning from their first mission, they understood more deeply that religion is, after all, purely a matter of personal experience [138:2.1], and they recognized the wisdom of the Master's plan of having them work in a quiet and personal way before public activity [138:2.10].

5. What Kind of Men the Apostles Were

It is a mistake to regard the apostles as altogether ignorant. All except the Alpheus twins were graduates of the synagogue schools, and seven of them came from the Capernaum synagogue school, the best in Galilee [139:0.3]. They merely lacked rabbinic tradition and higher education [139:0.4]. The apostles learned of the kingdom of heaven from Jesus, and Jesus learned much about human nature from them [139:0.2]. The fact that, although Jesus repeatedly shattered their personal ambitions, only one of them deserted him is a testimony to the charm and righteousness of his life [139:0.1].

Summary

The twelve apostles consisted of six chosen directly by Jesus and six recommended by them, and they were organized around Andrew, dividing their roles according to their talents [138:2.2, 138:10.2]. This approach shows that Jesus trained the apostles as leaders by trusting them from the beginning and sharing responsibility with them [138:1.3].

q304.question: Why was Judas Iscariot chosen as an apostle, and what led him to betray Jesus?
q304.answer:
Judas Iscariot was the twelfth apostle, chosen by Nathaniel, and as an able treasurer he carried out that office honestly and faithfully until his betrayal [139:12.1, 139:12.3]. The Urantia Book finds the cause of his betrayal not in money but in defects of character: an exaggerated sense of self-importance, accumulated resentment, and failure in spiritual growth [139:12.5, 139:12.6, 139:12.8].

1. What Kind of Man Judas Was

He was born in Kerioth and grew up in Jericho, and his Sadducee parents disowned him when he became a disciple of John [139:12.1]. He was thirty years old when he joined the apostles, probably the best-educated man among the twelve, and the only Judean [139:12.2]. He was a good thinker but not always a truly honest thinker; he did not really understand himself and was not really sincere in dealing with himself [139:12.2]. The apostles loved him and regarded him as a matchless treasurer and a learned man [139:12.5].

2. Why He Was Chosen: A Faith Adventure

From the beginning Jesus fully understood the weakness of this apostle and the dangers of admitting him. The Urantia Book says: "⟦Q 139:12.7⟧Para Jesus, Judas foi uma aventura com a fé.⟦/Q⟧." [139:12.7] For it is the nature of the Sons of God to give every created being a full and equal chance for salvation and survival, and it is their invariable practice fully to receive the candidate even when there are doubts about the sincerity of his devotion [139:12.7]. The door of eternal life is wide open to all, and there are no qualifications save the faith of the one who comes [139:12.7]. That is why Jesus permitted Judas to go on to the very end, doing everything possible to transform him [139:12.8].

3. The Roots of the Betrayal: Upbringing and Character

Judas was raised as the pampered only son of unwise parents; he overestimated his own importance and was a poor loser [139:12.6]. He developed the habit of indulging hatred and suspicion, misinterpreting the words and acts of his friends, and getting even with those he thought had mistreated him [139:12.6]. He never rose above his Judean prejudice against his Galilean associates, and he inwardly criticized Jesus as being timid and afraid to assert his power [139:12.4].

4. Failure in Spiritual Growth, and Resentment

Judas grew intellectually regarding Jesus' teachings, but unlike the other apostles he did not make progress in acquiring spiritual character [139:12.8]. The Urantia Book warns: "⟦Q 139:12.8⟧Contudo, quando a luz não é recebida com honestidade e vivida de acordo, ela tende a transformar-se em trevas dentro da alma.⟦/Q⟧." [139:12.8] Brooding over personal disappointments, he became the victim of resentment [139:12.9], and when his public protest was disallowed after a woman broke an expensive box of incense at Jesus' feet, the hate, jealousy, and revenge of a lifetime were mobilized [139:12.10]. He made up his mind to get even with he knew not whom, and he crystallized all that evil upon the one innocent person [139:12.10]. Jesus warned him many times, so far as was consistent with moral freedom, but divine warnings are usually futile with a nature steeped in bitterness [139:12.11]. The Urantia Book states plainly that money could never have been the motive for his betrayal [139:12.5].

5. The Tragic End and Its Lesson

While carrying out his plan of betrayal he experienced moments of regret and shame and faintheartedly conceived the idea that Jesus might at the last moment deliver himself by his own power [139:12.12]. When it was all over he fled from the realities of mortal existence by suicide, and Jesus regarded the betrayer only with pity [139:12.13, 139:12.14]. The case of Judas illustrates the truthfulness of the saying, "⟦Q 139:12.5⟧“Há um caminho que parece o justo para um homem, mas o fim dele é a morte”.⟦/Q⟧" [139:12.5].

Summary

Judas was received as a "faith adventure" in keeping with God's principle of giving everyone an equal chance [139:12.7], but because he failed to master his exaggerated self-importance and resentment and did not live up to the light he received, he came to betray Jesus [139:12.8, 139:12.11]. His story gives the solemn lesson that intellectual understanding alone is not enough: we must deal honestly with disappointment and hurt and cultivate spiritual character.
